advances: This gives an exact structural classification of every convex body whose real fibers are translates of the prescribed radial cube over the full \(\ell_1\) ball. After an affine shear preserving the mixed lattice, mixed volume, and every closed-cap depth, the entire class consists of the centers \(B|x|\) with \(|B_{li}|\leq1\). Thus this matrix family exhausts the common-radius cube class. The classification holds for all \(n,d\geq1\), and also identifies its intrinsic centroid residual rank. It makes no depth lower-bound claim for this entire class or for the locked general problem.
author: research-agent
proof:
For each continuous coordinate \(l\), define the actual upper and lower fiber extrema \(U_l(x)=c_l(x)+a(x)\) and \(L_l(x)=c_l(x)-a(x)\). These are finite and attained in the compact fibers, including their singleton boundary fibers. Given \(x,x'\in K\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), take a point realizing \(U_l(x)\) in \(C_x\), and one realizing \(U_l(x')\) in \(C_{x'}\). Convexity of \(C\) puts their convex combination in \(C_{(1-t)x+tx'}\), so

\[
U_l((1-t)x+tx')\geq(1-t)U_l(x)+tU_l(x').
\]

Repeating the argument for the minima gives \(L_l((1-t)x+tx')\leq(1-t)L_l(x)+tL_l(x')\). Thus \(U_l\) is concave and \(L_l\) is convex on the whole closed base. These inequalities are established from attained points of \(C\), without assuming continuity of \(c\).

Fix a sign vector \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\). Its closed orthant portion of the base is the simplex

\[
K_\sigma=\{x\in K:\sigma_ix_i\geq0\ (1\leq i\leq n)\}
=\operatorname{conv}\{0,R\sigma_1e_1,\ldots,R\sigma_ne_n\}.
\]

On all of this closed simplex, \(a(x)=R-\sum_i\sigma_ix_i\) is affine. Consequently concavity of \(U_l\) and convexity of \(L_l\) respectively imply concavity and convexity of \(c_l\) on \(K_\sigma\). Both inequalities together force exact Jensen equality for every segment in \(K_\sigma\). Applying this equality repeatedly to a finite convex combination gives its barycentric formula, since each \(x\in K_\sigma\) has coefficients \(|x_i|/R\) at \(R\sigma_ie_i\) and \(1-\|x\|_1/R\) at zero:

\[
c(x)=c(0)+\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{|x_i|}{R}\bigl(c(R\sigma_ie_i)-c(0)\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

For positive \(x_i\), the coefficient of \(|x_i|\) in (1) is \((c(Re_i)-c(0))/R=A_{\cdot i}+B_{\cdot i}\). For negative \(x_i\), it is \((c(-Re_i)-c(0))/R=-A_{\cdot i}+B_{\cdot i}\). Formula (1) therefore gives \(c(x)=c(0)+Ax+B|x|\) on every closed orthant simplex, hence on \(K\). These same axis values force the two displayed column formulas, proving uniqueness.

This also proves all compatibility and regularity assertions directly. A coefficient for coordinate \(i\) in (1) depends only on \(\sigma_i\) and the axis value \(c(R\sigma_ie_i)\), so it is independent of every unrelated sign flip. When \(x_i=0\), its term vanishes. Thus on any face where some coordinates are zero, all possible choices of their signs give the identical formula, with only the nonzero coordinates contributing. The right side \(c(0)+Ax+B|x|\) is continuous on \(K\). The proof of (1) already used the actual values at all boundary vertices and applies when \(\|x\|_1=R\), where the coefficient at zero is zero. There is therefore no assumed extension from an open orthant to its boundary. More explicitly, if \(x_k\to x\in\partial K\) and \(y_k\in C_{x_k}\), then continuity of this formula and \(a(x_k)\to0\) give \(y_k\to c(x)\). The ambient limit \((x,c(x))\) lies in \(C\) by its compactness and agrees with its prescribed singleton fiber. For \(n=1\), the closed simplices are exactly \([0,R]\) and \([-R,0]\); (1) proves the two affine pieces and their common value at zero in the same way.

To prove the coefficient bounds, the boundary points \((Re_i,c(Re_i))\) and \((-Re_i,c(-Re_i))\) both belong to \(C\). Their midpoint belongs to \(C_0=c(0)+[-R,R]^d\). For every \(l,i\), this gives

\[
\left|\frac{c_l(Re_i)+c_l(-Re_i)}2-c_l(0)\right|\leq R,
\]

which is precisely \(|B_{li}|\leq1\).

For the converse, suppose these entrywise bounds hold and define the fibers using \(c(x)=c(0)+Ax+B|x|\). Their coordinate endpoints are

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_l(x)&=c_l(0)+\sum_iA_{li}x_i-R+\sum_i(B_{li}+1)|x_i|,\\
U_l(x)&=c_l(0)+\sum_iA_{li}x_i+R+\sum_i(B_{li}-1)|x_i|.
\end{aligned}
\]

Every coefficient \(B_{li}+1\) is nonnegative, so \(L_l\) is convex; every coefficient \(B_{li}-1\) is nonpositive, so \(U_l\) is concave. The set \(C\) is the intersection of \(K\times\mathbb R^d\) with all epigraph constraints \(y_l\geq L_l(x)\) and hypograph constraints \(y_l\leq U_l(x)\), and is therefore convex. These functions are continuous, so this set is closed. Its base is compact, its center function is bounded on that base, and \(0\leq a(x)\leq R\), so it is bounded and compact. Its fibers are nonempty for every \(x\in K\), proving its projection is exactly \(K\). At \((0,c(0))\), the base inequality and every endpoint inequality are strict because \(R>0\). Continuity supplies an ambient open neighborhood in \(C\), proving full dimension. This also shows full dimension follows from the original hypotheses after their centers have been classified.

The map \(F\) has affine inverse \(F^{-1}(x,y)=(x,y+c(0)+Ax)\). Its base coordinate is unchanged, while on every real fiber it is a translation. Hence it maps \(\Lambda\) bijectively to \(\Lambda\), despite the matrices having arbitrary real entries, and sends the fibers of \(C\) to the displayed fibers of \(C_B\). For measurable \(E\subseteq\Lambda\), write \(E_z=\{y:(z,y)\in E\}\). Its section over each \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) is translated by \(-c(0)-Az\). Translation invariance of \(d\)-dimensional volume in each fiber and the locked sum formula give

\[
\mathcal H_d(F(E))
=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\operatorname{vol}_d\bigl(E_z-c(0)-Az\bigr)
=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\operatorname{vol}_d(E_z)
=\mathcal H_d(E).
\tag{2}
\]

To check closed halfspaces explicitly, write a proper one as \(H=\{(x,y):\alpha\cdot x+\beta\cdot y\geq t\}\) with \((\alpha,\beta)\ne0\). In the image coordinates it becomes

\[
F(H)=\{(x,y):(\alpha+A^{\mathsf T}\beta)\cdot x+\beta\cdot y\geq t-\beta\cdot c(0)\}.
\tag{3}
\]

Its normal is nonzero: if \(\beta\ne0\) this is immediate, and if \(\beta=0\) then \(\alpha\ne0\). The inverse map gives a bijection on all proper closed halfspaces, preserving containment of the corresponding points. Any whole-space or empty improper halfspaces are also preserved. Since \(F(S\cap H)=S_B\cap F(H)\), equation (2) proves the closed-cap volume identity. Taking infima over the bijection of containing halfspaces proves \(h_{S_B}(F(p))=h_S(p)\) for every \(p\in S\).

The positive fibers of either body are exactly those with \(\|z\|_1<R\): there their side length is \(2a_z>0\), on the base boundary they are singletons of zero \(d\)-volume since \(d\geq1\), and outside the base they are empty. The support is finite and contains zero, whose volume is \((2R)^d>0\). Symmetry of each cube about its center identifies its actual centroid and yields \(w_z=(2a_z)^d\). The identity \([-a_z,a_z]^d=(2a_zI_d)[-1/2,1/2]^d\) gives exactly the shape normalization of accepted fact `5e81b94633eacd39`, under the aliases in the statement. It also verifies the root weight \(w_z^{1/d}=2a_z\). These are actual volume weights for both bodies, preserved by the shear.

Finally, use only the affine selector and residual-rank conventions of accepted fact `ae8bb1ec375ace78`. If \(s:\operatorname{aff}(D_+)\to\mathbb R^d\) is affine for the original centroids, then \(s_B(z)=s(z)-c(0)-Az\) is affine for the sheared centroids and

\[
c_z-s(z)=c_{B,z}-s_B(z).
\]

The correspondence \(s\leftrightarrow s_B\) is bijective, so every residual span and the minimized ranks agree. When \(0<R\leq1\), the positive support is \(\{0\}\), its affine dimension is zero, and choosing the constant selector equal to its centroid gives rank zero. When \(R>1\), it contains \(0\) and \(\pm e_i\) for every \(i\), so its affine dimension is \(n\). The graph of the sheared centroids contains \((0,0)\) and \((\pm e_i,B_{\cdot i})\). The differences and sums of the latter points yield \((e_i,0)\) and \((0,B_{\cdot i})\) in its linear span. Thus its affine hull contains \(\mathbb R^n\times\operatorname{im}B\). Every graph point \((z,B|z|)\) already belongs to this space, so its affine dimension is exactly \(n+\operatorname{rank}B\). The rank identity (16) of accepted fact `ae8bb1ec375ace78`, with its centroid volume \(a_z\) identified as our \(w_z\), now gives \(r_{\mathrm{aff}}(D_+)=\operatorname{rank}B\). This proves every assertion without invoking any general depth estimate.
statement:
Let \(n,d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(R>0\). Write \(|x|=(|x_1|,\ldots,|x_n|)^{\mathsf T}\), \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_1\leq R\}\), and \(a(x)=R-\|x\|_1\). Suppose \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) is compact and convex, its base projection is exactly \(K\), and for every real \(x\in K\) its fiber is

\[
C_x:=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}=c(x)+[-a(x),a(x)]^d.
\]

This hypothesis includes the singleton fibers \(C_x=\{c(x)\}\) whenever \(\|x\|_1=R\), and imposes no initial regularity assumption on \(c:K\to\mathbb R^d\). Then there are unique matrices \(A,B\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}\) such that \(c(x)=c(0)+Ax+B|x|\) for every \(x\in K\), and they satisfy \(|B_{li}|\leq1\) for all \(1\leq l\leq d\), \(1\leq i\leq n\). Their columns are explicitly

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{\cdot i}&=\frac{c(Re_i)-c(-Re_i)}{2R},\\
B_{\cdot i}&=\frac{c(Re_i)+c(-Re_i)-2c(0)}{2R},
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(e_i\) is the \(i\)-th base coordinate vector. In particular \(c\) is continuous on the whole closed base, including every coordinate face and its boundary.

Conversely, for every \(c(0)\in\mathbb R^d\), \(A,B\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}\) satisfying these entrywise bounds, the set with precisely these fibers is a compact full-dimensional convex body with projection \(K\).

Let \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\), \(S=C\cap\Lambda\), and define the affine bijection \(F(x,y)=(x,y-c(0)-Ax)\). Then \(F(\Lambda)=\Lambda\), and

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_B:=F(C)&=\{(x,y):x\in K,\ |y_l-(B|x|)_l|\leq a(x)\ (1\leq l\leq d)\},\\
S_B:=F(S)&=C_B\cap\Lambda,\\
\mathcal H_d(F(E))&=\mathcal H_d(E)\quad\text{for every measurable }E\subseteq\Lambda,\\
\mathcal H_d(S_B\cap F(H))&=\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\quad\text{for every closed ambient halfspace }H,\\
h_{S_B}(F(p))&=h_S(p)\quad(p\in S).
\end{aligned}
\]

Here depth and mixed volume have exactly the meanings in the locked problem. For the sheared body, put \(c_{B,z}=B|z|\), \(a_z=R-\|z\|_1\), and

\[
\begin{aligned}
D_+&=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:\|z\|_1<R\},\\
(C_B)_z&=c_{B,z}+T_z[-1/2,1/2]^d,\qquad T_z=2a_zI_d\quad(z\in D_+),\\
w_z&=\operatorname{vol}_d((C_B)_z)=(2a_z)^d,\\
W&=\mathcal H_d(S_B)=\mathcal H_d(S)=\sum_{z\in D_+}w_z>0.
\end{aligned}
\]

The exact normalization aliases to accepted fact `5e81b94633eacd39` are its \(a_z,T_z,w_z,W,D_+\) equal to those displayed here, and its \(c_z\) equal to our \(c_{B,z}\) when describing the sheared fibers. Its original root weights are again \(w_z^{1/d}=2a_z\), rather than a probability law. The particular body of that fact is the subcase \(d\geq n\) with \(B_{li}=1\) if \(l=i\leq n\), and \(B_{li}=0\) otherwise.

For the original body, write \(c_z=c(z)\), its actual fiber centroid on \(D_+\). Use precisely the intrinsic centroid rank convention of accepted fact `ae8bb1ec375ace78`:

\[
r_{\mathrm{aff}}(D_+)=
\min_{s:\operatorname{aff}(D_+)\to\mathbb R^d\ \mathrm{affine}}
\dim\operatorname{span}\{c_z-s(z):z\in D_+\}.
\]

That predecessor's centroid volume denoted \(a_z\) equals our \(w_z\), not our radius \(a_z\). Its \(\rho_E\) and \(r_{\mathrm{aff}}(E)\) retain their definitions. Its affine hull denoted \(A\) in equation (6) is written \(\operatorname{aff}(E)\) here and is distinct from the coefficient matrix \(A\) of this theorem. With these aliases, the original and sheared bodies have the same intrinsic centroid residual rank on \(D_+\), and

\[
\bigl(\dim\operatorname{aff}(D_+),r_{\mathrm{aff}}(D_+)\bigr)
=
\begin{cases}
(0,0),&0<R\leq1,\\
(n,\operatorname{rank}B),&R>1.
\end{cases}
\]
